items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.

items.summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA

items.summary: This dataset provides a curated and reproducible compilation of data used to analyze long-term trends in external-cause mortality in Ecuador from 1990 through 2024. The primary data sources are official mortality statistics and population estimates and projections published by Ecuador’s National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos, INEC). The dataset includes annual mortality counts and population-based indicators for major external-cause categories, including land transport injuries, other transport accidents and accidental injuries, suicide, homicide, events of undetermined intent, and other external causes. Where available, the data are organized by calendar year, sex, age or age group, geographic unit, ICD classification, and cause of death. Population denominators, crude mortality rates, confidence intervals, absolute and relative changes, mortality composition measures, sex-specific rate ratios, and variables used in the statistical analyses are documented separately from the original source data. The repository also contains information used to support the reproducibility of the associated scientific study, including analytical datasets, variable definitions, ICD harmonization information, population denominators, model-related variables, sensitivity-analysis data, quality-control documentation, data provenance, and records of differences identified between historical editions of INEC statistical tables. Hospital discharge datasets reviewed during data curation are documented at the variable and source level. Individual-level hospital discharge microdata are not included in the public dissemination package when their inclusion could create unnecessary privacy or re-identification risks. Original source information is kept distinct from derived variables and researcher-calculated indicators to preserve full provenance and auditability. The package follows FAIR data principles and includes machine-readable CSV files together with the original curated Excel database, a data dictionary, methodology documentation, provenance and transformation records, quality-control information, ethics and privacy considerations, citation metadata, licensing information, and version history. No missing values were imputed solely for publication, and no undocumented assumptions were used to generate unavailable data. Values for recent years should be interpreted according to the provisional or revised status indicated by the original INEC sources. This dataset is intended to support reproducibility, secondary epidemiological analyses, public health surveillance, methodological review, and research on injuries, violence, suicide, homicide, road traffic mortality, and other external causes of death in Ecuador.
items.title: Ecuador External-Cause Mortality, Population Denominators, and Reproducibility Dataset, 1990–2024

items.summary: We present SemRepo, an RDF knowledge graph comprising over 81 million triples describing nearly 200,000 GitHub repositories associated with scientific research. SemRepo captures repository-level metadata, such as contributors, issues, and programming languages, and interlinks this information with external scholarly knowledge graphs. In particular, repository authors are linked to their profiles in SemOpenAlex, repositories are connected to scholarly publications in LPWC, and research artifacts, such as datasets and experiments, are linked via MLSea-KG. This integration enables queries that span publications and their scholarly artifacts, which are typically fragmented across separate platforms. SemRepo supports analyses that are difficult to perform with existing resources in isolation, including provenance reconstruction across repositories and publications, as well as the systematic identification of risks to research reproducibility and software sustainability. By unifying research software with its scholarly context in a single graph, SemRepo provides an important infrastructure for large-scale analysis of software within the broader scientific research ecosystem.
items.title: SemRepo: A Knowledge Graph for Research Software and Its Scholarly Ecosystem

items.summary: Reproducibility package for the manuscript "Distinct conformational and interaction signatures of the FGFR1 V561M and N546K resistance-associated mutations: a multi-replicate molecular dynamics study" . This package contains everything needed to regenerate every table, figure and reported number in the manuscript from the analysis outputs, except the raw trajectories. Systems and sampling: three FGFR1 kinase domain systems (wild type, V561M, N546K) in complex with erdafitinib, three independent 500 -ns replicates each , analysed over the 200 -500 ns plateau. Nominal sampling 4.5 us; realised aggregate production sampling 4.491 us. All three systems share a 9.28387 nm cubic SPC water box with 0.15 M NaCl (total atoms 78 , 608 / 78 , 609 / 78 , 624 ). Contents: - scripts/ - 14 analysis and plotting scripts (Python 3.10 ) covering every main and supplementary figure panel - tables/ - 38 per-replicate and summary result tables (CSV) - matrices/ - 24 DCCM matrices, common-subspace PCA projections and RMSD series (NumPy .npy) - mdp/ - GROMACS run-control files (minimisation, ions, NVT, NPT, production) plus the fully expanded grompp parameter file - tpr/ - the nine production run inputs (complete, with all parameters baked in ) - topology/ - GROMACS topology files ( system and protein topologies, posre.itp, ligand parameters, index files ) - README.md - directory layout, frame-selection rules, uncertainty conventions, table/figure provenance, and full run parameters Software: GROMACS 2024.6 (production) and 2024.3 (analysis), gmx_MMPBSA 1.6 .5 , MDTraj 1.10 .3 , Python 3.10 (NumPy 2.2 .6 , SciPy 1.15 .2 , Matplotlib). Frame selection: MM/GBSA and MM/PBSA energies were computed on frames extracted at 1-ns spacing ( 301 frames per intact replicate ; 291 for V561M replicate 2 ). Replicate-level statistics use one value per independent trajectory ( n = 3 per system ) and are reported as mean +/- SD ; frames within a trajectory are not treated as independent samples . Per-residue decomposition values are reported as mean +/- SEM , which can be converted to SD by multiplying by the square root of 3 . Important for regeneration: the production runs were executed as a 200 -ns run followed by a 300 -ns extension (gmx convert -tpr -extend). md.mdp therefore defines only the first 200 ns and must be read together with that extension step. See README.md section 7. Raw trajectories (approximately 13 GB, full atom resolution, 100 -ps output cadence) are available from the corresponding author on request .

The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. items.summary: This dataset provides a curated and reproducible compilation of data used to analyze long-term trends in external-cause mortality in Ecuador from 1990 through 2024. The primary data sources are official mortality statistics and population estimates and projections published by Ecuador’s National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos, INEC). The dataset includes annual mortality counts and population-based indicators for major external-cause categories, including land transport injuries, other transport accidents and accidental injuries, suicide, homicide, events of undetermined intent, and other external causes. Where available, the data are organized by calendar year, sex, age or age group, geographic unit, ICD classification, and cause of death. Population denominators, crude mortality rates, confidence intervals, absolute and relative changes, mortality composition measures, sex-specific rate ratios, and variables used in the statistical analyses are documented separately from the original source data. The repository also contains information used to support the reproducibility of the associated scientific study, including analytical datasets, variable definitions, ICD harmonization information, population denominators, model-related variables, sensitivity-analysis data, quality-control documentation, data provenance, and records of differences identified between historical editions of INEC statistical tables. Hospital discharge datasets reviewed during data curation are documented at the variable and source level. Individual-level hospital discharge microdata are not included in the public dissemination package when their inclusion could create unnecessary privacy or re-identification risks. Original source information is kept distinct from derived variables and researcher-calculated indicators to preserve full provenance and auditability. The package follows FAIR data principles and includes machine-readable CSV files together with the original curated Excel database, a data dictionary, methodology documentation, provenance and transformation records, quality-control information, ethics and privacy considerations, citation metadata, licensing information, and version history. No missing values were imputed solely for publication, and no undocumented assumptions were used to generate unavailable data. Values for recent years should be interpreted according to the provisional or revised status indicated by the original INEC sources. This dataset is intended to support reproducibility, secondary epidemiological analyses, public health surveillance, methodological review, and research on injuries, violence, suicide, homicide, road traffic mortality, and other external causes of death in Ecuador.

items.summary: This technical note investigates whether operator-relative noncentrality can predict the relative empirical power of complementary localized scan statistics in correlated spectra. The motivating real-data benchmark compares BABAR and BESIII measurements of the e⁺e⁻ → π⁺π⁻ cross section in the ρ-resonance region on a common 5 MeV grid from 0.600 to 0.880 GeV. The real-data comparison remains negative, with no statistically supported localized shape tension identified. The methodological study compares a coherent-yield scan with a covariance-profiled shape scan and defines the frozen coordinate Θ = log(ES/EY), where ES and EY represent maximum local operator-accessible signal strengths. An archival confirmatory replication used 50,000 null calibration draws per covariance environment, 15,000 independent null-validation draws per environment, 1,440 signal/covariance conditions, and 576,000 injected pseudoexperiments. Θ predicted which scan had greater empirical power with pooled AUC 0.9820 and mean leave-one-covariance-environment-out AUC 0.9740; its correlation with the empirical power difference was 0.9185. Independent Type-I error estimates ranged from 0.0466 to 0.0540. The results support operator-relative noncentrality as a useful empirical coordinate for complementary globally calibrated scans within the tested benchmark. The underlying ingredients, including Gaussian noncentrality, covariance-weighted subspace detection, quadratic scanning, and Monte Carlo calibration, are established; the contribution is a reproducible computational synthesis and controlled characterization rather than a claim of a new general statistical law
items.title: Operator-Relative Noncentrality in Localized Correlated-Spectrum Scans: A BABAR–BESIII Benchmark

items.summary: Topic models, in particular Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), have been adapted to hyperspectral imagery (HSI) as a route to interpretable spectral mixtures: each spectral unit (canonically a pixel) becomes a document of quantised band-frequency tokens and the inferred topic-word distributions act as non-negative basis spectra. Yet the dominant evaluation criterion remains downstream classification accuracy, an accuracy-only view that is silent on whether the basis is reproducible, band-robust, calibrated, or actually outperforms standard linear baselines. We propose and instantiate a twelve-axis evaluation framework for LDA-style topic models on HSI that quantifies, on the same set of benchmarks: (F-1) classification macro-F1 compared across five method families (paired differences and a hierarchical Bayesian model), (F-2) topic-word coherence (c_v, c_NPMI, U-Mass), (F-3) seed stability for both LDA and two neural variants (ProdLDA, ETM), (F-4) capacity sensitivity across K in {4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16}, (F-5) band-mask robustness, (F-6) cross-method clustering agreement (LDA vs Felzenszwalb, SLIC, patches, pixels), (F-7) topic-label coupling via P(L | t) entropy and KL, (F-8) per-topic Hungarian-aligned identity tracking, (F-9) HIDSAG cross-preprocessing stability, (F-10) cross-scene topic transfer, (F-11) rate-distortion of the topic representation, and (F-12) external alignment of the topics with a spectral library and a method-rank cross-comparison. We apply the framework to six standard HSI benchmarks (Indian Pines, Salinas, Salinas-A, Pavia University, Kennedy Space Center, Botswana) and five subsets of the HIDSAG mineralogical database (GEOMET, MINERAL1, MINERAL2, GEOCHEM, PORPHYRY). The framework yields three findings that the accuracy-only view does not surface. First, on the labelled scenes the topic-routed soft classifier, which routes the raw spectrum to per-topic logistic experts, matches the raw-spectrum logistic baseline in macro-F1 (0.915 against 0.910, a paired difference of 0.005), while a logistic regression on the topic proportions theta alone trails the baseline by 0.325: the topics add an interpretable routing to the raw spectrum but do not replace it. Second, on Salinas-A under the SWIR-only band mask the paired ARI between canonical and masked dominant-topic maps reaches 0.766, while on Kennedy Space Center under every mask, and on Botswana under the SWIR mask, the same paired ARI collapses to approximately 0.01, separating scenes on which an interpretability claim is band-robust from scenes on which it is not. Third, the theta-only deficit holds on HIDSAG: over its nineteen mineralogical targets the topic-logistic classifier trails raw-logistic by 0.268 macro-F1 (lower on 18 of 19 targets), contrary to the prima-facie expectation that mineralogical mixtures favour topic decomposition over the raw spectrum. We release 3895 deterministic derived artefacts (449 MB), the builder source, the FastAPI backend, the React frontend, and a 109-endpoint test harness as a public, MIT-licensed reproducibility package. items.summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA

items.summary: Hashing Is Not Retrieval is a prospectively frozen three-arm evaluation of context accumulation in small-model multi-agent code cartography. It compares three ways for an orchestrator to hand work to a worker: 1. FULL HISTORY — retransmit prior worker outputs. 2. OPAQUE REF — replace the previous output with an unretrievable SHA-256 digest. 3. RETRIEVED — resolve the digest through a tenant-scoped content-addressed store and inject the recovered bytes. All arms receive identical source-derived evidence. The apparatus measures the exact message content sent to workers and records token counts, model and provider identifiers, generation IDs, usage, cost, retries, and retrieval proofs. A five-task gate preceded a fixed 50-task controlled benchmark, followed by a separate state-required evaluation across 24 deterministic fixtures and a five-scale Medusa case study. Key result: in the controlled benchmark, RETRIEVED reduced paired peak context by 38.3% relative to FULL HISTORY. The state-required follow-up shows that opaque references fail when state must be recovered, while verified retrieval preserves substantially more structural information. This is bounded-context evidence for automatic orchestrator-resolved state passing inside a specific two-worker code-cartography harness — not a universal claim about autonomous memory, long-context capability, or reasoning quality. The release includes the corrected author-identified preprint, executable apparatus, frozen results, task fixtures, telemetry, and verification instructions. Version 1.0.2 supplies the curated, verifier-passing reproducibility archive. It supersedes the uncurated archive from version 1.0.1 and includes the exact pinned apparatus, state-required fixtures, frozen results, and archive verifier. items.summary: This work studies whether internal rotation changes the longevity of source-free localized excitations in the reduced Enchan local time-rate field. The frozen scalar dynamics are S_tt = div[mu(D) grad S] - S with D = |grad S| and mu(D) = 1/(1 + D^(3/2)); no continuing external torque, centrifugal force, primitive matter source, or added rotational potential is used during the reported evolutions. Stage A supplies the non-rotating source-free baseline. Stage B1 initializes rotating phase-space states at omega = 4, 8, and 12 and evolves the extended runs to dimensionless time t = 100. Over 80 <= t <= 100, the mean localized-energy fractions are approximately 0.002207 for the non-rotating baseline and 0.006006, 0.149470, and 0.368846 for omega = 4, 8, and 12. The result is a graded rotation-associated longevity hierarchy: weak rotation gives little practical rescue, intermediate rotation substantially extends localization, and the strongest tested branch remains transient-localized through t = 100. Matched-energy near-zero-J_z controls provide a separate causality check and show that net canonical angular momentum alone is not a monotonic explanation of every late-time difference. Stage B2 separately tests spontaneous self-spin from exactly zero initial total angular momentum and finds no validated convergent counter-rotating branch in the tested scalar-only initial-data families. The ordered scan supports a physical formation picture in which a localized grain can move from weak rotational asymmetry through progressive spin-up into a strong-rotation long-lived branch. Time, space, and omega are dimensionless reduced-branch quantities; t = 100 is not assigned an SI duration in this work. The deposit contains the Version 1.0 manuscript PDF, a reproducibility ZIP with the publication source, code, selected archived numerical outputs, README, LICENSE, and SHA-256 integrity manifest. The final main.pdf is the default preview. License: Enchan Research & Verification License v1.0. Copyright (c) 2026 Mitsuhiro Kobayashi.

items.summary: This repository contains the data, documentation, and replication materials associated with the data paper on the  Cartulario de Santo Toribio de Liébana . The dataset provides a structured reconstruction of the documentary collection edited by Luis Sánchez Belda and converts the information contained in the cartulary into machine-readable research data. It covers 566 documentary acts and includes linked information on 576 payment or counter-performance elements, 603 place names, and 1,348 identified persons , together with a concordance between documentary numbering systems. The package preserves the documentary structure of the source while providing standardized variables suitable for quantitative and computational historical research. Particular attention is given to economic transactions. Payments and other forms of material counter-performance are recorded at the individual-component level rather than collapsed into a single transaction value. The data also distinguish operative contractual provisions from penalty clauses and other formulaic diplomatic material. Contains the materials required to reproduce and audit the construction of the dataset, including the structured datasets, extraction and coding documentation, variable definitions, provenance information, validation materials, and the code used for data processing and quality-control procedures. The replication workflow documents the transformation from the published documentary source to the final structured tables. It records corrections and normalization decisions while maintaining traceability to the underlying documentary act. The package is therefore intended not only to reproduce the published dataset but also to make individual coding decisions auditable. The dataset is designed for reuse in research on medieval economic history, property transactions, monastic institutions, historical geography, social networks, and computational approaches to diplomatic sources.

items.summary: Cyber threats directed against space systems (spanning orbital payloads, tracking and telemetry ground stations, downlinks, and upstream manufacturing supply chains) have evolved into acute operational hazards. Concurrently, national security and commercial defenders face an intelligence volume crisis where telemetry and vulnerability disclosures outpace human cognitive bandwidth. While autonomous multi-agent pipelines powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) offer scalable automation, they introduce severe epistemic liabilities: hallucination, source detachment, uncalibrated certainty, and susceptibility to indirect prompt injection. This paper presents Space-Cyber Brief Crew, a multi-agent cyber threat intelligence (CTI) architecture that automates space-domain intelligence synthesis under an explicit governance layer. Built on a decoupled CrewAI orchestration, the system routes structured reporting through a three-stage sequential pipeline (Collector, Analyst, Writer) governed by ten operational rules. Crucially, the architecture establishes a structural boundary between action capabilities and generative synthesis: downstream analysis agents operate in zero-tool sandboxes, restricting the execution attack surface by construction. We evaluate the framework against a tri-domain threat corpus spanning satellite imagery manipulation, ground industrial control systems (ICS), and global navigation satellite system (GNSS) spoofing. In our evaluation, the governed architecture eliminated identifier fabrication (from 23.3% to 0.0%), preserved 100% provenance retention, and neutralized indirect prompt injection attacks that succeeded in 80% of unconstrained baseline runs. Finally, we examine the institutional, regulatory, and oversight implications, establishing technical criteria for federal procurement and intelligence integration.

items.summary: This deposit contains the analysis code, fitted parameters, output files, audit records, supplements, and citation list supporting the working paper "Power-Law Claims in Production and Supply Networks: What Survives a Uniform Certification Audit" (version 16, September 2026, posted on SSRN) by Bruce Rishel (Independent Scholar, ORCID 0009-0000-8324-4331) and Melissa Rishel (Independent Scholar, ORCID 0009-0001-4919-0728). Melissa Rishel contributed the independent validation of the statistical analysis and the mathematical derivations. The audit applies the Clauset-Shalizi-Newman 2009 maximum-likelihood estimation protocol with semi-parametric bootstrap goodness-of-fit testing and likelihood-ratio tests against alternative distributions, together with the Broido-Clauset 2019 five-category corpus classification, to a verified population of 20 published power-law claims in the supply chain operational literature. Three widely cited datasets are re-analyzed. The manuscript reports four distributions: Acemoglu et al. 2012's sectoral input-output out-degree (BEA 1997 Use Table), Liu, Shen, Tan 2021's international trade product networks in both the out-degree and in-degree directions (BACI HS92 Y2024 current release, 1,217 networks), and Axtell 2001's US firm-size distribution (SUSB 2017, n = 5,996,900 firms via the Virkar-Clauset 2014 binned-data MLE). The Acemoglu influence vector is analyzed separately and treated as exploratory, described under the version note below. The remaining 17 audit targets are characterized at methodology rigor level without independent data re-analysis. items.summary: A three-signal stopping rule for iterative LLM refinement derived from the Möbius theory stack: an equilibrium-distance surrogate d̂_R (RZGM meaning-equilibrium layer), an update-free-recurrence and diversity-collapse detector pair (Reflective Homeostasis Layer), and a hard reflection-depth cap (MUSE bounded reflection). Pre-registered study: 500 English prose-refinement tasks across ten domains, two generator models (Gemma4 12B-IT-QAT and 26B-A4B-IT-QAT), 8,000 generations, 999 blind position-swapped pairwise judgments. The governor cuts refinement tokens by 36.6% / 33.1% (bootstrap 95% CIs 33.6-39.5% / 30.3-35.9%) versus an always-eight-iterations baseline — 2.2-3.4x a naive convergence stop — at a measured quality cost reported at equal prominence: 38.0% / 36.6% of judged comparisons lost overall, a majority among actual interventions (61.1% / 59.0%), with measured cost almost perfectly collinear with output length. A full-data ablation shows the saturation signal is simultaneously the savings engine and the dominant cost source, yielding a measured two-point dial (10.0-11.5% savings at 8.2-11.8% loss rate with saturation disabled). Pre-release adversarial verification (four independent refuter passes) confirmed all headline statistics against the raw data and caught an inverted flagship anecdote: the corpus's two catastrophic degenerations (~50 verbatim paragraph repetitions) were selected once and avoided once by the governor, undetected in both cases — set-based trigram signals are structurally blind to within-output verbatim repetition. All tasks, rollouts, verdicts, audit votes, and analysis code are released in the companion repository. items.summary: We present SemRepo, an RDF knowledge graph comprising over 81 million triples describing nearly 200,000 GitHub repositories associated with scientific research. SemRepo captures repository-level metadata, such as contributors, issues, and programming languages, and interlinks this information with external scholarly knowledge graphs. In particular, repository authors are linked to their profiles in SemOpenAlex, repositories are connected to scholarly publications in LPWC, and research artifacts, such as datasets and experiments, are linked via MLSea-KG. This integration enables queries that span publications and their scholarly artifacts, which are typically fragmented across separate platforms. SemRepo supports analyses that are difficult to perform with existing resources in isolation, including provenance reconstruction across repositories and publications, as well as the systematic identification of risks to research reproducibility and software sustainability. By unifying research software with its scholarly context in a single graph, SemRepo provides an important infrastructure for large-scale analysis of software within the broader scientific research ecosystem.
items.title: SemRepo: A Knowledge Graph for Research Software and Its Scholarly Ecosystem

items.summary: A mineral prospectivity map stacks geophysical, geochemical and structural evidence over a study area and outputs, per cell, the probability that a deposit is there. Such maps are typically presented with an area-under-curve (AUC) and a posterior, and both numbers can be inflated in two specific, well-understood ways. ProspectMap is an interactive tool that computes such a map by Weights of Evidence, a Bayesian log-odds update, and makes those two inflations first-class, measuring them rather than hiding them. This report quantifies both on the real US Midcontinent Mississippi-Valley-type zinc-lead belt (the open Critical Minerals Mapping Initiative dataset of Lawley et al., 2022) and on ten synthetic cases. The first inflation is evaluation: reporting AUC under random cross-validation, which lets spatially adjacent cells leak between train and test, overstates prospective skill. On the real belt, with thresholds, weights and prior fitted on the training folds only and every map cell scored, the Weights-of-Evidence AUC falls from 0.74 under random cross-validation to 0.65 under spatial block cross-validation, an inflation of 0.09, the second largest of the eleven cases. Under the same spatial folds a learned classifier reaches 0.91, but a baseline that ranks cells by their distance to the nearest training deposit reaches 0.90, so this protocol does not show that the classifier learned more than proximity to known deposits. The second inflation is modelling: Weights of Evidence assumes the evidence layers are conditionally independent given a deposit, and on the real belt they are not. The posterior probabilities sum to 1124 against 858 deposit cells (omnibus z = 8.3), so the posterior is overconfident. The six layers' contrasts are individually significant (studentized contrasts 2.45 to 5.80; exact one-sided p ≤ 1.9 × 10⁻³), but four of them come from thresholds that leave no deposit outside the pattern, where the weight outside the pattern is set by a zero-count correction. The tool displays the spatial-CV AUC, the conditional-independence test and the per-layer significance beside the inflated values; every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive tool and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_ProspectMap . Interactive tool: https://prospectmap.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: Critical Minerals Mapping Initiative US Mississippi-Valley-type Zn-Pb belt dataset (Lawley et al. 2022, doi:10.1016/j.oregeorev.2021.104635).

items.summary: This work studies how small perturbations of the Enchan local time-rate field propagate through fine spatial structure in the same field. The problem is motivated by the hard-wall boundary used in a previous Enchan two-route interference study: rather than imposing a primitive material opacity or an S=0 wall, the present work asks whether finite structure in the Enchan field itself can generate scale-selective transmission and reflection. Starting from the reduced finite-tension branch S_tt = div[mu(D) grad S] - S with mu(D) = 1/(1 + D^(3/2)), the field is decomposed as a structured background plus a small propagating perturbation. Stage A uses a predeclared one-dimensional frozen structured background and compares it with a matched smooth/homogenized control. The response is banded rather than a monotonic low-pass: long-scale perturbations remain comparatively transmissive while strong reflection bands appear when the perturbation resolves the fine structure. At ka = 2 the mean Stage-A structured transmission is approximately 6.25e-4 while the smooth control remains approximately 0.989; at ka = 4 the structured transmission is approximately 1.07e-14 while the smooth control remains approximately 0.962. Stage B replaces the hand-constructed surrogate with three previously frozen source-free Enchan final states from the published localized-field study. The source files are SHA-256 checked against the original run manifest before analysis. All three source profiles remain within the declared positive longitudinal branch and reproduce a scale-dependent structured-versus-smooth transmission difference. The largest Stage-B mean differences occur near ka = 1.0 and 1.5, where structured transmission is approximately 0.330 and 0.358 while the smooth controls remain approximately 0.994 and 0.988. The maximum Stage-B conservation residual is approximately 1.89e-15. Stage C extends the test to a full three-dimensional propagation study using the same three previously frozen source-free Enchan field configurations. A total of 54 cases were evaluated across structured, smooth, and vacuum controls, three selected spatial scales, and both normal and 30° oblique incidence. The scale-dependent scattering observed in the one-dimensional diagnostics persists in three dimensions. Structured backgrounds show reduced forward transmission together with increased reflection and lateral scattering relative to the matched controls. At ka = 4 under normal incidence, the mean structured transmission is approximately 0.486, compared with approximately 0.527 for the smooth control and 0.532 for vacuum. The maximum three-dimensional energy-accounting residual remains below 1.2% across all 54 cases. The result supports a model-level statement: fine S-field structure can act as a wavelength-selective barrier for small time-rate perturbations within the declared linearized Enchan branch. It does not identify ordinary matter with the tested surrogate or source-free structures, does not claim monotonic high-frequency blocking, and does not claim that a macroscopic material wall has been reconstructed. The Zenodo deposit contains the Version 1.1 manuscript PDF together with the complete reproducibility package for Stages A, B, and C, including the frozen numerical code, Stage-C configuration, archived source states, full numerical results, summary tables, execution manifest, README, LICENSE, and SHA-256 integrity records. The manuscript PDF is generated directly from the final Version 1.1 TeX source and is set as the default Zenodo preview. Version 1.1 update: Version 1.1 adds the completed Stage-C three-dimensional validation, updates the manuscript and reproducibility package accordingly, and preserves the Stage-A and Stage-B results unchanged. items.summary: Benchmark package accompanying the manuscript “Failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems: residual-error decoupling, an attainable-accuracy bound and an identifiability benchmark”. The package contains: the exact solution of the beam–two-mass moving-load benchmark and the modal and RK4 reference baselines on the same grid; the training campaign with random seeds, network configurations, collocation densities, training budgets, measured wall-clock times, residuals and relative-L2 errors for every run; the inverse-problem (speed and load-amplitude) campaign with its identifiability verdict; the weights of the reference physics-informed network; and the scripts that regenerate every figure, table and number of the paper. It supports two results of the paper: the residual–error decoupling for moving singular sources, and the attainable-accuracy bound obtained by fitting the same architecture to the exact solution. All runs are seeded, so the accuracy–cost comparison reported in the paper can be re-derived without retraining.
items.title: Benchmark package — failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems (v1.0)

items.summary: README – Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics (CGMD) Simulations of PIEZO1 and TRPM4 Overview This dataset contains coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) simulations of the mechanosensitive ion channel PIEZO1 and the non-mechanoprotective ion channel TRPM4 embedded in lipid bilayers. The simulations comprise 500 ns of equilibrium followed by membrane stretching simulations designed to investigate how PIEZO1's distinctive triskelion blade architecture redistributes mechanical stress and preserves membrane integrity. All simulations were performed using GROMACS with the Martini 3 force field. Independent replicate simulations (n = 3) were conducted for each system to ensure statistical robustness and reproducibility. Simulation Details Parameter Description Molecular dynamics engine : GROMACS v2021.2 Force field : Martini 3 Membrane model : Lipid bilayer containing either PIEZO1 or TRPM4 Equilibration : 500 ns Stretching simulations : Three independent replicates (n = 3); 50 ns Simulation temperature, pressure, and all additional parameters are provided in the accompanying simulation input files (.mdp) and described in the associated publication. Biological Significance PIEZO1 is a mechanosensitive ion channel whose unique triskelion blade architecture protects cellular membranes from mechanical failure. Its extended peripheral blades redistribute mechanical stress across the lipid bilayer, reducing localized stress accumulation and delaying membrane rupture during mechanical loading. This dataset enables quantitative investigation of how membrane protein architecture influences membrane mechanics, force redistribution, and mechanoprotection using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. Dataset Structure 1. Equilibrium Simulations These simulations characterize the equilibrated membrane environment surrounding each ion channel before mechanical loading. Simulation length: 500 ns PIEZO1_equilibrium.pdb PIEZO1_equilibrium.xtc TRPM4_equilibrium.pdb TRPM4_equilibrium.xtc 2. Membrane Stretching Simulations Following equilibration, membrane stretch was induced using semi-isotropic pressure coupling, with −5 bar applied in the membrane plane (x–y) while maintaining +1 bar normal to the bilayer (z-axis) using the Parrinello–Rahman barostat.
